reasons: Lake identity record confirms United States v. Jeremy Payne, Ninth Circuit, decided 2024-04-17, docket 22-50262.
Lake citation display and selected official citation are 99 F.4th 495, matching the page citation and year.
The opinion centers on suspicionless parole searches under California parole search conditions and the Fourth Amendment reasonableness framework.

The case is materially about a supervision-search exception: the panel held the general parole search condition independently authorized the cell-phone search and that Riley did not govern parole searches of a cell phone.
residual_risks: The disclosed files do not include the target home page's own criteria for the label Key, so this review verifies subject-matter fit rather than a comparative corpus ranking.

reasons: The opinion states that California's general suspicionless search condition is mandated by law and that it subjected Payne's property to search with or without warrant or cause.

The opinion holds that Payne's statutorily mandated general search condition independently authorized the cell-phone search and that any ambiguity from the special condition did not make the search unreasonable.
The opinion expressly says: "Parole searches, on the other hand, require no such probable cause determination as to the place or thing being searched."
The opinion rejects Payne's Riley argument because Johnson had rejected applying Riley to parole searches of a cell phone, and it declined to extend Riley's reasoning here.
The Fifth Amendment portion holds that using Payne's thumb required no cognitive exertion, was not testimonial, and therefore the Fifth Amendment did not apply.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: To avoid overbreadth, preserve the qualifier that officers still needed probable cause to believe Payne was on active parole and subject to an applicable search condition.
